final.title: Measuring late payment terms without guessing
final.body:
If you want to measure late payment terms, keep the decision narrow: are you still tracking due dates, agreed terms, actual payment dates, and follow-up status by memory or spreadsheet, or do you already have a repeatable check that flags overdue invoices before they turn into a cash-flow surprise?

That is the part worth automating first. Not the whole finance process, just one recurring task: compare invoice date, agreed terms, and payment date; flag anything past due; and keep a simple log of what was late. Any collection action still stays with a human. Money movement stays human too.

The useful filter is simple: how many invoices do you issue each month, and how do you currently know which ones are late? If the answer depends on manual review or memory, that workflow is worth looking at. If it is already reliable and low-effort, automation may not earn its place.

A practical next step is to audit one week of invoices. Note which were paid on time, which were late, and how long the manual review took. That gives you a bounded picture of the work before you decide whether a pilot is worth setting up. Small business finance is rarely mysterious; it is usually just unhelpfully handwritten.
